# Canonical lifts preserve complete lattice intersections

This structural lemma identifies information that must be retained after
the arbitrary-finite-base target was disproved in
`candidate 640d07cd1de2a423`.
It supplies no quantitative depth estimate. the contributor proof; audit pending.

## 1. A finite lattice-complete base and its representation space

Let U be a nonempty finite subset of Z^n such that

    conv(U) intersect Z^n=U.                         (1)

Let L(U) be the vector space of scalar functions f:U->R satisfying

    f(u)=sum_v alpha_v f(v)

for every anchored convex representation

    u=sum_v alpha_v v, alpha_v>=0, sum_v alpha_v=1.   (2)

This vector space has a basis with rational values at every point of U.
Indeed, for each u the coefficient vectors in (2) form a bounded
polytope defined by a rational matrix and rational right side. A vertex
is obtained by selecting a linearly independent subsystem of the active
linear equations, including zero coordinates, and solving it; its
coordinates are rational by elimination. There are finitely many such
vertices. Each representation is a convex combination of these vertices,
so it is enough to impose the equalities for this finite list. Thus
L(U) is the kernel of a finite rational matrix. Row reduction provides
the claimed rational basis.

The constant function and the original coordinate functions belong to
L(U). Choose finitely many additional rational functions spanning L(U)
together with them, and multiply each added function by an appropriate
positive integer so its values on U are integers. Define

    Psi(u)=(u,f_1(u),...,f_k(u)) in Z^(n+k).          (3)

The coordinates together with the constant span L(U), so this is
affinely equivalent to the canonical lift formed from any basis of L(U)
modulo constants. More explicitly, each coordinate in either construction
is an affine function of the coordinates in the other, on the respective
affine hulls. These maps are inverse on the spanning finite sets, hence
on their affine hulls. The first n coordinates of Psi are the original
u, so no two original sites are identified.

## 2. No new lattice points appear in the lifted hull

The integer-coordinate lift satisfies

    conv(Psi(U)) intersect Z^(n+k)=Psi(U).           (4)

To prove this, write a point w of the left side as
sum_v alpha_v Psi(v). Its first n coordinates are an integer point
u=sum_v alpha_v v in conv(U). By (1), u belongs to U. This is one
of the anchored representations (2), so every added coordinate obeys
sum_v alpha_v f_j(v)=f_j(u). Consequently w=Psi(u). The reverse
inclusion is immediate.

Put E=aff(Psi(U)), choose u_0 in U, and set

    E_0=E-Psi(u_0),
    Lambda_0=E_0 intersect Z^(n+k).

This is a full-rank lattice in E_0. It contains r=dim(E) linearly
independent integer differences of points of Psi(U), which span E_0.
Here is an elementary basis argument. The subgroup Lambda_0 is
saturated in the ambient integer lattice: if a nonzero integer multiple
of an integer vector lies in E_0, then that vector itself lies in E_0.
Divide any nonzero member by the gcd of its coordinates; saturation
keeps the resulting primitive integer vector in Lambda_0. Integer
Euclidean row operations send it to the first coordinate vector.
Subtracting integer multiples of that vector from every other member
splits off a Z factor. The remaining subgroup in the last coordinates
is again saturated, and its real span has dimension r-1. Induction
supplies a basis of r integer vectors, and sends Lambda_0 to
Z^r times zero coordinates by an ambient unimodular transformation.
The case r=0 is the one-point case. This proves the lattice assertion.

Thus with the affine lattice Lambda=Psi(u_0)+Lambda_0, equation (4)
says

    conv(Psi(U)) intersect Lambda=Psi(U).             (5)

Choosing a lattice basis identifies E with R^r and Lambda with Z^r.
Under this affine identification, the canonical lifted configuration
is again a complete lattice intersection in its convex hull.

## 3. Closed minors and the original positive fibers

If P is finite and conv(P) intersect Z^n=P, and U=P intersect conv(U),
then conv(U) intersect Z^n=U. Indeed an integer point of conv(U)
belongs first to P and then to its closed trace U. Therefore the lemma
applies to every closed minor used in the archived canonical-minimum
reduction. It also applies after successive such operations.

For the original positive-d-volume mixed fibers, their base set P is
lattice-complete. If an integer z is a convex combination of positive
fiber bases, take one positive coefficient alpha at a full-dimensional
source fiber and fixed points in the other source fibers. Convexity puts
a translate of alpha times that source fiber in C_z, so C_z has positive
d-volume. Hence conv(P) intersect Z^n=P. Zero-volume original boundary
fibers need separate intrinsic handling, as in the archived reductions;
they are not used in this positive-volume argument.

## 4. What this preserves, and what it does not prove

The canonical lift preserves anchored representations in both directions:
one direction is (2), and the reverse is projection to the original
coordinates. It therefore preserves convex traces and the finite Helly
number, as in the earlier canonical-lift source. The construction above
adds that the lifted point configuration has some full-rank lattice for
which it is a complete convex intersection. That property is absent from
the unequal three-site counterexample.

The lattice rank r after lifting can exceed the original integer
dimension n. This lemma does NOT replace the requested factor2^(-n)
by2^(-r), or identify the lattice with the original mixed-integer lattice.
In a finite-base argument one still tracks the original bound h(P)<=2^n
and the exactly preserved finite Helly number. A sharp theorem involving
that number for lattice-complete configurations is a separate unproved
claim. The point of (5) is to retain an arithmetic constraint that cannot
be discarded in favor of h(P) alone.

Arbitrary projective changes of the base preserve the convex traces but
need not preserve (5). On a line they can turn three equally spaced
sites into the ratio1:99 configuration of the exact counterexample.
The projective unweighted orbit is consequently not an admissible
replacement for the original lattice-complete class when seeking its
sharp numerical bound.

## 5. Every pairwise congruence, in particular parity, is preserved

For the integer-coordinate lift (3), for all u,v in U and every positive
integer m,

    Psi(u)-Psi(v) in m Lambda_0
          if and only if u-v in m Z^n.              (6)

The forward implication follows by projection onto the first n integer
coordinates. For the reverse, assume m>=2 and u-v is divisible by m.
The point w=v+(u-v)/m is both an integer point and a point of conv(U),
so w is in U by (1). Preservation of this anchored representation gives

    f_j(u)-f_j(v)=m(f_j(w)-f_j(v))

for each added coordinate. Thus Psi(u)-Psi(v) is divisible by m in
the ambient integer lattice. Its quotient lies in E_0 as well, and
hence in Lambda_0. The case m=1 is immediate. This proves (6).

Let k(U) be the number of congruence classes modulo2 met by U in its
original integer lattice. Equation (6) gives exactly the same number
of occupied parity classes in the lifted affine lattice Lambda, even
if its rank r exceeds n. In particular

    k(Psi(U))=k(U)<=2^n.                             (7)

This is stronger bookkeeping than merely bounding the new lattice's
rank and then paying2^r. The initial parity count is preserved exactly.

## 6. Additivity on dependence components

Use the dependence components of the archived canonical reduction:
in every anchored convex representation, its target and every source
with positive coefficient belong to one component. Equivalently these
components are the connected components of the hypergraph of such
nontrivial representations. Distinct components of a lattice-complete
U occupy disjoint parity classes.

Indeed, if u and v in different components had the same parity, their
midpoint w would be an integer point of conv(U), hence a point of U.
The representation w=(u+v)/2 would place u,v,w in one component,
a contradiction. Therefore if the components are U_1,...,U_l,

    k(U)=sum_i k(U_i).                               (8)

Every closed minor T has k(T)<=k(U), simply by inclusion, and the
canonical lift preserves that value by (7).

Consequently the *conditional attained-counterexample reduction* can
also be run with target gamma_d/k(U) on lattice-complete bases,
instead of the false unrestricted target gamma_d/h(U). Here is the
precise dependency. If OC fails for one original positive-volume base
P in Z^n, its depth is strictly below gamma_d/2^n and hence strictly
below gamma_d/k(P). Among the finitely many canonical lifted closed
minors choose one violating its own gamma_d/k(U) target with smallest
cardinality. Splitting into components and retaining the component
with M_i/k(U_i)>=M/k(U) contradicts minimality, by (8) and the
archived exact depth restriction inequality. A normalized minimizing
sequence cannot lose all mass on any proper complement: its positive
limiting-mass set T is closed, retained mass tends to one, and
k(T)<=k(U), giving a smaller bad minor by the same restriction and
canonical-lift inequalities. Thus all limiting fiber masses are
positive. The remaining diameter propagation, affine-shear normalization,
compactness, and depth continuity are exactly those proved in Sections6-7
of `candidate c280bb0dcfd30f3d`; their proofs do
not use the numerical choice of h(U) rather than k(U).

This supplies an attained all-positive dependence-connected bad minimum
with its finite arithmetic base and its original occupied-parity budget
retained. It does NOT prove the sharp gamma_d/k(U) target at that minimum.
That restricted numerical theorem is a new remaining obligation, not
a consequence of (6)-(8) or of ordinary Helly alone. No arbitrary
projective changes of the base are included in this reduction.

For a nontrivial rank-increasing calibration, the thirteen-point example
in `candidate e3932c47b953f7cd` has original
lattice rank3 and canonical lift (p,g(p)) of rank4. The integer lift
is full-dimensional in R^4, remains lattice-complete, and occupies
exactly8 parity classes rather than all16. The separate exact verifier
`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_canonical_lift_lattice_parity_root.py` enumerates its rational
supporting facets and every integer point in its bounding box, and
checks these assertions and all pairwise congruences through modulus7.
The general proofs above, not this finite check, establish the lemma.

## 7. The remaining minimum contains a primitive three-site chain

At a positive minimum below gamma_d/k(U), every fiber has volume
strictly below M/k(U): otherwise its ordinary centroid alone attains
the required raw depth gamma_d M/k(U). Hence |U|>k(U), since summing
at most k(U) such strictly smaller volumes could not give M.
Some parity class therefore has two distinct sites.

After identifying the inherited lattice with Z^r, choose a same-parity
pair p,q in U with the smallest Euclidean distance. Write q-p=2v,
v in Z^r. The vector v is primitive. If v=mw for an integer m>=2,
the lattice point p+2w lies on the segment[p,q], and hence in U by
lattice completeness. It has the same parity as p and is strictly
closer, contradicting the choice. Thus U contains the three consecutive
sites p,p+v,p+2v on a primitive lattice line. The middle site belongs
to a different parity class, since a primitive integer vector is not
twice an integer vector. The midpoint fiber contains the actual
Minkowski average of the two endpoint fibers.

This is a structural consequence only. It does not transfer all source
mass to that triple or prove a sharp depth bound there for the full
family. In particular, the archived midpoint-tree and forest-cap
counterexamples prohibit treating repeated averaging as additive mass
accounting. Global deepest points can also share a parity class; the
exact faceted plateau source remains a counterexample to that shortcut.
